title: India Extends Solar Cell Sourcing Exemption to December, Buying Time for Domestic Manufacturing
excerpt: The MNRE's six-month extension of the ALMM-II waiver for net metering and open access projects could unlock up to 10 GW of stalled installations, but the gap between module and cell manufacturing capacity remains a structural challenge.
body:
• India has extended the exemption from mandatory domestic solar cell sourcing (ALMM List-II) for net metering and open access projects until December 31, 2026, up from the earlier May 31 deadline.
  • The extension could help commission up to 10 GW of pending solar projects currently held up by procurement constraints, according to industry estimates.
  • India's domestic solar cell manufacturing capacity stands at roughly 18-30 GW against nearly 200 GW of module capacity, creating a severe supply-demand mismatch.
  • Projects commissioned after December 31, 2026, will be required to comply with ALMM List-II provisions, with no further blanket extensions planned.

India's Ministry of New and Renewable Energy has extended a critical exemption allowing net metering and open access solar projects to use imported solar cells until December 31, 2026, offering relief to an industry grappling with a widening gap between ambition and domestic manufacturing capacity.

The decision extends a waiver that had previously been available until May 31 under the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) framework, which mandates that government-backed solar projects source components from approved domestic manufacturers. The ministry made clear this is a limited transition window — not a blanket reprieve — and that all projects commissioned from January 2027 onward must comply with ALMM List-II requirements for solar cells.

A Supply Chain Under Strain

The extension addresses a fundamental structural problem in India's solar ecosystem. While the country has built an annual solar module manufacturing capacity of nearly 200 GW — one of the largest in the world — domestic solar cell production lags far behind at an estimated 18 to 30 GW, depending on how operational capacity is measured.

This mismatch has left hundreds of standalone module manufacturers, which assemble panels but do not produce cells, scrambling for supply. At least three solar module makers have temporarily halted production for lack of domestically made cells, while four more have cut capacity to about a third, according to Reuters.

"It is impossible to start producing cells with 18 months' notice due to complicated technology, manufacturing needs like land and sourcing raw materials."

— Chetan Shah, Chairman, Solex Energy

The situation has direct cost implications. Industry estimates suggest the extension could lower EPC costs for eligible projects by approximately ₹7,000-8,000 per kilowatt-peak, depending on configuration. Domestic cells currently cost about ₹28 per watt-peak compared with ₹14-14.5 for imported cells, largely sourced from China, according to Mint.

10 GW of Projects in the Balance

Industry stakeholders say the extension is critical for projects already in the pipeline. Ashok Kumar Singh, an independent solar consultant, estimated that nearly 10 GW of projects currently being handled by over 100 EPC players could now be commissioned by December because of the additional time.

Simarpreet Singh, CEO of Hartek Power, noted that past experience with ALMM List-I had shown how a limited approved-vendor base creates demand-supply asymmetries, leading to multi-week project delays. "The six months to implementation provide an adequate runway, provided enlisted cell capacity ramps up as projected and pricing stabilises through competition among approved manufacturers," he said.

The Road to Self-Reliance

Despite the extension, the government has maintained its broader policy direction. The ALMM framework, introduced in 2019, represents India's push to become self-reliant in solar manufacturing across the entire value chain. The ministry has already announced plans to extend domestic sourcing requirements to ingots and wafers under ALMM List-III from June 2028.

Industry experts project that domestic cell manufacturing capacity could reach 30-35 GW by December 2026 and 60-70 GW by the end of the next financial year, which would broadly align with India's annual demand of 30-40 GW for government-backed projects. However, much of the existing capacity uses older PERC technology, with only about 6-7 GW operating on the newer TOPCon technology that yields higher-efficiency cells.

"Domestic operational solar cell manufacturing capacity is currently around 18 GW. By December 2026, I expect it to increase to around 30-35 GW, which should broadly align with India's annual domestic demand."

— Ashok Kumar Singh, Independent Solar Consultant

What Comes Next

The standalone module manufacturing sector employs about 75,000 workers, including 45,000 in Gujarat alone, making the transition a politically sensitive issue. Industry leaders have called for longer-term policy visibility to support investment planning, with some suggesting a phased transition backed by regular capacity reviews would be more effective than fixed deadlines.

For now, the December deadline represents a hard line. The question is whether India's cell manufacturing capacity can scale fast enough to meet it — or whether the industry will be back at the negotiating table before year's end.
